primary_meaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'works of the law' (Greek: erga nomou) is Paul's shorthand for deeds performed in obedience to the Mosaic law regarded as a basis or means of justification before God. The dominant (especially Protestant/Reformation) interpretation extends this to human moral effort or works-righteousness generally: no one is declared righteous by performing what the law commands; justification comes instead through faith in Christ. The phrase thus symbolizes the failed path of self-achieved righteousness contrasted with grace received by faith.
primary_basis: Galatians 2:16 (three-fold denial that anyone is justified by works of the law)
Galatians 3:2-5 (receiving the Spirit by faith, not works of the law)
Galatians 3:10-11 (all who rely on works of the law are under a curse)
Romans 3:20 (by works of the law no flesh will be justified; through the law comes knowledge of sin)
Romans 3:27-28 (justified by faith apart from works of the law)
Romans 9:31-32 (Israel pursued the law as if by works, not by faith)
Philippians 3:9 (not having a righteousness of my own derived from the law)
Ephesians 2:8-9 (not by works, so that no one may boast — often cited as the broader principle)

alternatives.meaning: New Perspective on Paul (Sanders, Dunn, Wright): 'works of the law' refers primarily to Jewish identity/boundary markers — circumcision, food laws, Sabbath observance — that separated Jews from Gentiles. Paul's target is ethnic exclusivism (requiring Gentiles to become Jewish), not moral effort or legalism per se.
basis: Galatians 2:11-16 (context of table fellowship and Peter's withdrawal from Gentiles)
Galatians 5:2-6 and 6:12-15 (circumcision as the presenting issue)
Romans 3:29-30 (God is God of Gentiles also, immediately following 3:28)
Dead Sea Scrolls parallel 4QMMT ('some of the works of the law') cited as background

alternatives.meaning: Traditional Catholic/Thomistic reading: 'works of the law' means chiefly the ceremonial and judicial precepts of the Mosaic law (circumcision, sacrifices, dietary rules), now obsolete in Christ; the moral law remains binding, and works done in grace retain a role in salvation. Justification excludes ceremonial observance and unaided works, not grace-empowered obedience.
basis: Romans 3:28 read alongside James 2:24 ('a person is justified by works and not by faith alone')
Council of Trent, Session 6, and patristic/medieval exegesis (e.g., Jerome, Aquinas) distinguishing ceremonial from moral precepts

alternatives.meaning: Works of the law as anything done under the old covenant economy 'in the flesh,' i.e., apart from the Spirit — a salvation-historical reading in which the phrase marks the old era of the law versus the new era of the Spirit, rather than legalism or ethnic markers specifically.
basis: Romans 7:5-6 (serving in newness of the Spirit, not oldness of the letter)

alternatives.meaning: Subjective-genitive or 'works the law produces' reading: the phrase denotes what the law itself works or effects (e.g., knowledge of sin, condemnation), rather than human deeds of obedience. Held by a small number of scholars.
basis: Romans 3:20b (through the law comes knowledge of sin)
Grammatical arguments about the genitive construction erga nomou

notes: There is broad consensus that 'works of the law' refers in some way to observance of the Mosaic law in contrast to faith in Christ as the ground of justification; the live scholarly dispute concerns scope and target. The Reformation reading (works-righteousness/legalism generally) remains dominant in popular and confessional Protestant teaching, while the New Perspective reading (covenant boundary markers) is very influential in academic Pauline studies since the 1980s — arguably co-dominant in scholarship. The phrase is technically a theological expression rather than a symbol in the imagistic sense, so 'symbolic meaning' here is understood as its standard interpretive referent. Key occurrences of the exact phrase are confined to Romans 3 and Galatians 2-3.
